title: Which PowerShell are you running?
summary: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 live side by side on every Windows machine. Tell them apart, and make scripts say what they need.

steps.title: Two PowerShells on one machine
body: Every Windows 10 and 11 machine (and every Windows Server) has **two different programs** called PowerShell:
| | Windows PowerShell 5.1 | PowerShell 7 |
| Program | `powershell.exe` | `pwsh.exe` (`pwsh` on Linux and macOS) |
| Runs on | .NET Framework 4.x, Windows only | modern .NET, Windows, Linux, macOS |
| Comes with | Windows itself | you install it: `winget install --id Microsoft.PowerShell --source winget` |
| New features | none since 2016, only security fixes | every release |
| Default file encoding | UTF-16 for `>` and `Out-File`, the ANSI code page for `Set-Content` | UTF-8 without a BOM, everywhere |
As of November 2026 the versions that matter are **PowerShell 7.6**, the **LTS** release (built on .NET 10, March 2026,
supported until November 2028), and **PowerShell 7.7**, the newest stable release (.NET 11, November 2026, short-term
support). 7.4 and 7.5 went out of support on 10 November 2026. Most teams standardise on the LTS for servers and build
agents. The machine in these lessons runs **7.6 LTS** on Linux.
**Why it matters at work:** a script written in `pwsh` can fail in `powershell.exe` (and the other way round), and the
error rarely says "wrong PowerShell". A scheduled task, a CI agent or a colleague's shortcut may start the old one.
Windows PowerShell 5.1 is not going away: it ships in Windows and some Windows-only modules still need it.

steps.prompt: Which PowerShell is each fact about?
items: Runs on Linux and macOS too
Gets new cmdlets and fixes in every release
steps.explain: 5.1 is frozen: it only gets security fixes, in step with Windows. Everything new (`-Parallel`, `??`, `&&`, `$PSStyle`, UTF-8 by default) is PowerShell 7 only.

steps.prompt: A script works on your laptop. On a build server it fails at once with this. What is the most likely cause?
code: ForEach-Object : A parameter cannot be found that matches parameter name 'Parallel'.
options: The build agent runs the script with Windows PowerShell 5.1 (`powershell.exe`), which has no `-Parallel`
The server needs the ThreadJob module from the PowerShell Gallery
steps.explain: The `ForEach-Object :` prefix and the `At ... char:` position are how 5.1 prints errors; PowerShell 7 prints `ForEach-Object:` on one concise line by default. Fix the agent's task to run `pwsh`, and add `#Requires -Version 7.4` so the next mistake fails with a clear message.

steps.title: Ask the shell, then make scripts say what they need
body: `$PSVersionTable` tells you exactly what is running:
```powershell
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion          # 7.6.10
$PSVersionTable.PSEdition          # Core (PowerShell 7) or Desktop (Windows PowerShell 5.1)
[System.Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation]::FrameworkDescription   # .NET 10.0.x
$IsWindows; $IsLinux               # automatic booleans in PowerShell 7 (they do not exist in 5.1)
A script that needs PowerShell 7 should say so on its **first line**:
```powershell
#Requires -Version 7.4
`#Requires` is checked **before a single line runs**. In 5.1 the script then stops with a clear "requires version 7.4"
error, instead of a confusing parse error halfway through, after it may already have deleted something.
`#Requires -Modules Pester` and `#Requires -RunAsAdministrator` (Windows) work the same way.

steps.title: What is this machine running?
prompt: Your terminal is **PowerShell** (`pwsh`). Record what it runs, so a teammate can compare it with their laptop:
`Set-Content -Path FILE -Value VALUE` writes a value to a file, or pipe into it: `VALUE | Set-Content FILE`.

checks.name: version.txt holds the version
checks.fail: `~/answers/version.txt` should hold exactly the version, like `7.6.10`. `$PSVersionTable.PSVersion.ToString()` gives it as text.

checks.name: dotnet.txt holds the .NET description
checks.fail: Use `[System.Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation]::FrameworkDescription` and write its value into `~/answers/dotnet.txt`.

hints: Type `$PSVersionTable` first and look at the table.
`$PSVersionTable.PSVersion` is a `[version]` object; `.ToString()` turns it into `7.6.10`.
`$PSVersionTable.PSVersion.ToString() | Set-Content ~/answers/version.txt`, and the same pattern for the other two.
steps.explain: On Windows, run the same in both `powershell` and `pwsh` once: it is the quickest way to see the two side by side. `Desktop` means Windows PowerShell 5.1 on .NET Framework; `Core` means PowerShell 6 or later on modern .NET.

steps.prompt: Make the script refuse to run anywhere older than PowerShell 7.4, and print which edition it is on.
steps.explain: `#Requires` is a special comment, not a cmdlet: it must start the line with `#Requires`, and PowerShell reads it before running anything.

steps.prompt: `deploy.ps1` starts with `#Requires -Version 7.4`. Someone runs it with Windows PowerShell 5.1. What happens?
options: Nothing in the script runs: PowerShell stops with an error saying the script requires version 7.4
The script runs until the first PowerShell 7 feature, then fails
5.1 ignores the line because it is a comment
steps.explain: `#Requires` is checked when the script is loaded. That is the point: fail before any side effect. It does not switch shells for you; the caller has to run `pwsh -File deploy.ps1`.

steps.title: Make a PowerShell 7 script say so
prompt: `~/scripts/rotate.ps1` uses `??` and `ForEach-Object -Parallel`, which only exist in PowerShell 7. A colleague ran it
from Windows PowerShell 5.1 and got a parse error about `??` that took an hour to understand.
Make `#Requires -Version 7.4` its **first line**, keep the rest as it is, and run it: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/rotate.ps1`

checks.name: the first line is #Requires -Version 7.4
checks.fail: The very first line of `~/scripts/rotate.ps1` should be `#Requires -Version 7.4` (`Get-Content ~/scripts/rotate.ps1 -TotalCount 1` shows it).

checks.name: the script still runs
checks.fail: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/rotate.ps1` should still print `ok: rotated 3 logs`. Did the rest of the script survive?

checks.name: PowerShell refuses it on an older version
checks.fail: The `#Requires` line should make PowerShell stop before running anything when the version is too old.

hints: Read the file into a variable: `$body = Get-Content ~/scripts/rotate.ps1` gives an array of lines.
Put the new line in front: `@('#Requires -Version 7.4') + $body`.
`Set-Content ~/scripts/rotate.ps1 -Value (@('#Requires -Version 7.4') + $body)`, then `pwsh -File ~/scripts/rotate.ps1`. Or open it with `nano ~/scripts/rotate.ps1` and add the line on the page.
steps.explain: `pwsh -File script.ps1` is how schedulers and CI should start a script: a fresh process with the right shell. `-NoProfile` as well keeps your own profile out of it, so the script behaves the same everywhere.
